storm.summary_layperson: No thunderstorms anywhere nearby tonight — skies are clear — but the Weather Service has coastal flood and wind alerts up for tomorrow morning through Thursday, so watch for high tides and a windy Thanksgiving.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer buffer: the Sound (56°F) is already 11°F warmer than the air at 4 PM, and the air keeps cooling to ~36°F by 8 PM, widening that gap the wrong way all evening.
storm.detail_html:
Regional picture: KOKX radar shows no echoes to track and the atmosphere has no instability at all (CAPE 0 J/kg). A cold, dry north wind is blowing behind high pressure (1029–1030 hPa across the area). There is no thunderstorm threat tonight.

Why the risk reads moderate: the rating is driven entirely by active NWS products from Upton, not by convection. A Coastal Flood Statement covers minor tidal flooding around Wednesday morning’s high tide, a Coastal Flood Watch runs Thursday into Friday, and a Wind Advisory takes effect Thursday morning. None of these begins during tonight’s 5–10 PM window.

Local effect — none in play: the cove’s usual storm buffer depends on the air being at least ~5°F warmer than the Sound, which keeps a cool, stable layer sitting on the water. Tonight it’s reversed. The Sound is 56°F, the air is about 45°F, and the model cools the air to ~36°F by 8 PM, so the gap goes from −11°F to about −20°F. With no stable layer and no sea breeze (sunset was 4:29 PM, and the wind is offshore anyway), the cove behaves like everywhere inland.

What would change the call: nothing convective is expected in this pattern. The things to watch are the coastal flood timing at the next high tides and how the Thursday wind advisory develops. Check the NWS statements for tide heights before leaving a boat or car near the waterfront.

wind.regime_label: Light north gradient wind after dark — no sea breeze
wind.tactics_blurb: A light, puffy north breeze blowing off the land with no sea breeze, 6–8 kt all evening. Stay center and sail the shifts. Puffs come off the Greenwich shore in streaks, so keep your head out of the boat and tack on headers.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Wind type: light gradient wind, no sea breeze. This is a gradient-wind day, not a sea-breeze day. The air is about 11°F colder than the Sound (air–water temperature difference −11°F), so there’s no thermal engine. Sunset is 4:29 PM, so the whole 5–10 PM window is after dark anyway. Every station around western Long Island Sound reads north (median 349°, no southerly readings anywhere), driven by high pressure to the northwest.

Speeds: RYC reads 8 kt gusting 11 (10-minute average 6 kt) and the mid-Sound buoy reads 11 gusting 17. The model keeps the cove at 6–8 kt through 8 PM. The cove sits in the lee of the land on a north wind, so expect less than mid-Sound, and expect it to fade a little after dark as the air near the ground cools and settles. Times after 8 PM are beyond the model run and are held at the current trend.

Shift character: north–northwest wind comes off the land, so it’s gusty and shifty, with 15–30° oscillations as puffs roll down from Greenwich. Neighborhood stations disagree a lot at low level (directions scattered NE to W, gusts 2–3× the average speed). That tells you the breeze is patchy close to shore. Expect holes.

Where the pressure is: with offshore wind the breeze generally builds as you move away from the shore, and puffs arrive in streaks rather than as a steady side advantage. There’s no persistent shift to bank on, so stay near the middle of the course and sail the oscillations instead of banging a corner.

What the fleet will feel: 6–8 kt with puffs to 10–12 means a light-to-medium night. Boats will be fully powered in the puffs and slow in the lulls. Air temperature drops from the mid-40s to the upper 30s through the window, with the wind adding chill. Dress for cold, not for the breeze.

data_caveats: HRRR 20Z run only reached 8 PM (forecast hours 6–12 unavailable); 9 PM and 10 PM wind values are persistence estimates.
Model output has no gust field; gusts estimated from RYC and buoy gust ratios.
Storm risk is 'moderate' only because of active NWS coastal flood and wind products (effective Wednesday–Thursday); no convection expected tonight.
